character_and_relationship_context: Aminata Diallo is a young woman from Bamako who works as the only female and the youngest member on a construction crew. She lives frugally in a rented room with a kerosene lamp, walks long distances to save bus fare, and studies accounting at night. She keeps a hidden emergency fund and a notebook of figures, never spends savings unnecessarily, and guards her plans, including her goal of finding a room with running water for her younger sister. She is precise, silent, and trusted by coworkers who do not know her family history: her mother died when she was twelve after a miscalculated loan ruined her market stall; her father sold his tools for a funeral and never worked again. Her master mason Sékou calls her la petite comptable because she recalculates load-bearing estimates mentally. Among coworkers, Moussa is the only one who occasionally covers for her when she arrives late from studying, and he has never asked for repayment. In past situations, she has declined social invitations when a study deadline was near, but has also attended work-related gatherings when she judged the goodwill worth the lost study time.
objective_situation: After a long day at the construction site, Aminata's coworker Moussa tells her that his family is hosting a celebration tonight for the birth of his first child. He insists she come, saying the whole neighborhood will be there. Aminata remembers that at such events, young women are often expected to sit with the elders and help serve tea while the men talk. She is exhausted and has studying to do, but she also values the goodwill of her coworkers. Moussa is waiting for her answer as she finishes packing her tools.
state_and_available_memories: Her shoulders ache from stacking blocks all day, her stomach is empty because she skipped lunch to save money, and her study lamp has no extra kerosene. Immediate memory: Moussa's mention of the celebration makes her recall a similar event last year where she was asked to serve tea and missed the last bus home, forcing her to walk two hours. Reflective memory: She remembers that her mother often attended neighborhood gatherings even when exhausted, and those relationships later provided loans and child care after her father left.
name: Aminata Diallo
